options.text: A custom type that defines a common group of related choices in a type-safe way.
options.explanation: Right. Swift enums define a fixed set of related values with strong type safety.

options.text: A dynamic reference class that automatically inherits properties from NSObject.
options.explanation: Enums are value types and do not inherit from classes.

options.text: A system collection that stores unordered key-value pairs like a dictionary.
options.explanation: Dictionaries store key-value collections; enums define distinct cases.

options.text: A memory pointer used to manage concurrent thread locks across CPU cores.
options.explanation: Enums are high-level data types, not concurrency thread locks.

questions.prompt: How do Swift enums differ from enums in C or Objective-C by default?

options.text: Swift enums cannot be matched inside exhaustive switch statements without a fatal crash.
options.explanation: Swift enums work smoothly with exhaustive switch statements.

options.text: Swift enum cases do not receive integer values by default unless explicitly specified.
options.explanation: Right. Unlike C, Swift enum cases are distinct values in their own right without default numbers.

options.text: Swift enums are dynamic reference types allocated on the heap alongside class instances.
options.explanation: Swift enums are value types, not reference types on the heap.

options.text: Swift enums can only define up to two cases maximum per individual file declaration.
options.explanation: Swift enums can declare as many cases as needed.

questions.prompt: Are Swift enumerations value types or reference types?

options.text: They are reference types shared across all scopes in the application.
options.explanation: Swift enums are value types, not reference types.

options.text: They are reference types when containing associated values, but value types otherwise.
options.explanation: Enums are always value types regardless of their associated values.

options.text: They are value types, meaning they are copied when assigned or passed to functions.
options.explanation: Right. Enums are value types and are copied on assignment.

options.text: They are dynamic types that transition to pointers when stored inside an array.
options.explanation: Enums maintain value semantics when stored in collections.

questions.prompt: Why must a switch statement over a Swift enum be exhaustive?

options.text: To enable the compiler to convert all cases into mathematical integers.
options.explanation: Exhaustiveness is for program correctness, not integer conversion.

options.text: Because Swift switch statements do not support default fallback branches.
options.explanation: Swift switch statements support default branches when needed.

options.text: To satisfy the Objective-C runtime protocol inheritance requirements.
options.explanation: Exhaustiveness is a native Swift type-safety guarantee.

options.text: To prevent uncaught states from executing, ensuring complete compile-time safety.
options.explanation: Right. Requiring exhaustive matching guarantees no unhandled case causes a runtime bug.

questions.prompt: What is an associated value in a Swift enumeration?

options.text: Custom data of any type attached to an enum case when an instance is created.
options.explanation: Right. Associated values let different cases store custom data varying per instance.

options.text: A fixed global integer assigned automatically by the compiler at compile time.
options.explanation: Fixed constants shared by cases are raw values, not associated values.

options.text: A static computed property shared equally by all cases in the enumeration.
options.explanation: Computed properties compute values, while associated values store per-instance data.

options.text: An internal memory address pointing directly to the parent module binary.
options.explanation: Associated values store payload data, not module addresses.

questions.prompt: What is a raw value in a Swift enumeration?

options.text: A mutable heap pointer created when an enum case is assigned to a variable.
options.explanation: Raw values are not heap pointers.

options.text: A predefined constant of a uniform type shared by all cases in the enum.
options.explanation: Right. Raw values prepopulate cases with fixed constants of the same type.

options.text: A temporary variable that changes value whenever a mutating method executes.
options.explanation: Raw values are immutable constants determined at compile time.

options.text: An unformatted string created by the debugger during an active breakpoint.
options.explanation: Raw values are a language feature, not debugger output.

questions.prompt: What is an enumeration in Swift, and how does it differ from enums in C or Objective-C? Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Defines a Swift enumeration as a type representing a group of related values
Explains that Swift enums do not assign integer values to cases by default
Mentions that cases are first-class values in their own right

questions.modelAnswer: In Swift, an enumeration defines a custom type for a fixed group of related values. Unlike enums in C or Objective-C, Swift enum cases do not receive integer values by default. Each case is a full, first-class value in its own right. Developers can optionally assign raw values or attach associated values to cases.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between raw values and associated values in Swift enums. Can an enum use both? Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that raw values are compile-time constants of a uniform type shared across all instances
Explains that associated values are custom data attached to individual instances at runtime
States that an enum cannot combine raw values and associated values

questions.modelAnswer: Raw values are predefined, compile-time constants of a uniform type shared by every instance of a case. In contrast, associated values are custom data payloads attached to individual instances when created at runtime. An enum cannot use both features at the same time. If an enum declares a raw type, its cases cannot take associated value arguments.

questions.prompt: Why does the raw value initializer init?(rawValue:) return an Optional in Swift? What must developers do when using it? Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that init?(rawValue:) is a failable initializer returning an Optional
States that it returns nil if the provided raw value does not match any valid case
Mentions that developers must safely unwrap the resulting optional value

questions.modelAnswer: The raw value initializer init?(rawValue:) is a failable initializer that returns an optional enum instance. It returns nil whenever the supplied raw value does not match any defined case in the enum. Because of this possibility, developers must safely unwrap the resulting optional using optional binding or optional chaining before accessing the case.

questions.prompt: Can Swift enums have properties and methods? What kind of properties are forbidden? Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that enums can declare instance methods, mutating methods, and computed properties
States that enums are forbidden from having stored properties
Mentions that per-instance data must be stored as associated values instead

questions.modelAnswer: Swift enums can include instance methods, mutating methods, type methods, and computed properties. However, enums cannot contain stored properties. The compiler produces an error if you attempt to declare a stored variable inside an enum. If an enum needs to store per-instance data, developers must use associated values instead.

questions.prompt: Why does Swift require switch statements on enums to be exhaustive? How does this protect code when new cases are added? Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that exhaustive matching ensures every possible enum case is handled
States that adding a new case produces a compile-time error in any switch without a default branch
Notes that this compiler check prevents uncaught cases and runtime logic bugs

questions.modelAnswer: Swift requires switch statements on enums to be exhaustive so that every possible case is handled. Adding a new case produces a compiler error at every switch statement lacking a default branch. This compile-time check forces developers to update their logic, preventing unhandled states and silent bugs.
